about: An enumeration of what an A1 Hindi candidate must be able to do. Two separate claims are stacked here and they have different strengths, so read them apart. THE POINT SET is derived structurally from core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, which restates the A1 inventory the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE -- a real awarding body, a published syllabus, finite and split into A1 and A2 columns. Spanish is used here as a PROXY FOR LEVEL: it is asked what an A1 learner must HANDLE, not what Spanish grammar it names, and each such demand is given the Hindi exponent that carries the same load. Every one of the proxy's 273 points is accounted for -- 264 are cited by some point's `derivedFrom`, and the remaining 9 are Spanish-typographic demands with no Devanagari counterpart, named with a reason in the generator. THE HINDI EXPONENTS are editorial throughout. Deciding that Spanish's `a` before a human object is answered by Hindi's `ko`, or that its drinking toast is answered by the shubh- formulas, is this project's judgement and nobody else's. ATTRIBUTE NOTHING TO DELE OR THE INSTITUTO CERVANTES ABOUT HINDI: they published a Spanish syllabus and have said nothing whatever about this language. Why a proxy at all: no Hindi awarding body publishes a content syllabus. core/exam-levels.json maps Hindi A1 to the Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha 'Prathmic' rung with basis 'editorial', and that was re-checked before this file was written. DBHPS publishes the NAMES of its examinations (Parichaya, Prathamic, Madhyama, Rashtrabhasha, Praveshika, Rashtrabhasha Visharad, Rashtrabhasha Praveen) and the prescribed readers, and no grammar inventory, no word list, no can-do descriptors and no A1/A2 split. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO DBHPS EITHER. Kendriya Hindi Sansthan and the Central Hindi Training Institute publish no level-split content inventory, and no Council of Europe Reference Level Description exists for Hindi. An earlier draft of this file built its point set from the CEFR Companion Volume's A1 descriptors alone and reached 172 points; measuring against a descriptor-derived list turned out to flatter the corpus, because descriptors are deliberately abstract where a syllabus enumerates. The proxy adds 110 points and drops none. Each point carries `derivedFrom`: either the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or `hindi-specific` for the 22 points that answer no Spanish demand at all -- the Devanagari script points, the postposition and oblique-case system, the nuqta, the register split, the karna compound verbs. A proxy is a scaffold, not a template to translate, and those 22 are why. Every scope dimension is `partial`, this inventory is NOT complete, and the coverage percentage it produces is a measure of the corpus against this list -- never an exam-readiness claim.
source: No awarding-body content syllabus exists for Hindi; see `about`. The point set is derived structurally from the project's own restatement of the DELE/PCIC A1 inventory at code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, whose own source is https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ele/plan_curricular/niveles/02_gramatica_inventario_a1-a2.htm and its sibling function, notion and orthography inventories. The Hindi exponents and the gap notes are bounded by the project's own checked-in A1 contract at https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/hindi/assessment-spec.md with hindi/task-shapes/a1.json and the two timed mocks in hindi/mocks/a1/. The DBHPS pages checked and found to publish exam names but no syllabus are https://www.dbhpscentral.org/Syllabus.html and https://dbhpscentral.org/examination.html (checked 2026-09-01).

communicative-functions.note: The proxy's functional column IS finite and level-split, which is what would close a dimension -- for Spanish. It does not close this one, because the exponent that realises each function in Hindi is our choice every time, and a function inventory without its exponents is half a source. All 54 proxy function points are answered here, plus two the proxy has no A1 slot for but the track's own A1 speaking construct scores: register choice and conversational repair. Where a checked-in A1 mock item pins an exponent down -- the cafe price turn, the sign-reading items, the named-reader message -- the point's note cites the item, and those are the strongest claims in the file.

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence and coordination columns) and https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/hindi/mocks/a1/
grammar.note: THE DIMENSION THE PROXY HELPS MOST, AND STILL DOES NOT CLOSE. There is no published Hindi equivalent of the PCIC grammar inventory, so before the proxy this column was built by reading every stimulus in the two checked-in A1 mocks and enumerating the construction each required -- a floor, since a construction absent from both mocks was absent from the list. Walking the proxy's grammar column raised that floor considerably: the article points surfaced that nothing tells a learner Hindi HAS no article; the reflexive-se point surfaced `apna`, which both mocks use and neither the descriptors nor a mock-reading had named; the direct-object-`a` point surfaced object-marking `ko`. It still does not close, because a demand Spanish does not make can still be an A1 demand in Hindi -- the oblique case and the ergative `ne` are the obvious ones -- and no source bounds those.

phonology-orthography.source: The Unicode Devanagari block (U+0900-U+097F) for the inventory of letters, code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json for the orthographic demands, and hindi/pronunciation-reference.md
phonology-orthography.note: The dimension where the proxy is LEAST useful, and it is worth saying why rather than quietly under-enumerating. Spanish's orthography column is about an alphabet the learner already has: accents, capitals, punctuation. Hindi's demand is a different writing system, so most of this column is `hindi-specific` and four of the nine untransferable proxy points are Spanish typography. Devanagari's letter inventory IS finite and enumerable, so the script points state exactly which letters the track has an atom for and which it does not, and the notes give the counts -- that half is nearly closed. Pronunciation is not: no source separates A1 Hindi phonology from A2, so contrasts, stress and intonation are enumerated on the project's judgement and left honestly unmapped where nothing teaches them. Drawing that A1/A2 line ourselves would be the editorial promotion the Spanish file itself declines to make, so this dimension stays partial for the same stated reason.

lexicon.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 36 general-notion and 77 specific-notion A1 points) and the topic areas named in hindi/assessment-spec.md
lexicon.note: No published A1 Hindi word list exists -- no DBHPS list, no Goethe-style Wortliste, no ranked frequency band adopted by any Hindi awarding body. What the proxy supplies is a bounded set of DOMAINS, which is a real improvement on topic areas we chose ourselves: the walk added shopping and payment, transport, free time, media, written correspondence, documents and educational institutions, every one of which the mocks test and none of which the earlier descriptor-derived draft enumerated. A domain point claims the track has a usable foothold in that domain, NOT that it holds the domain's full A1 vocabulary. No per-word count is claimed complete and none should be inferred: this file deliberately contains no 'holds N headwords' point, because a probe cannot honestly express one.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped. Every atom named in every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms the hindi track actually introduces; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point. A point the corpus cannot demonstrate gets `probe: null` and a note saying what is missing and, wherever the demand is written down, which checked-in A1 mock item makes it. One deliberate liberty is taken and named here so it is not a hidden generosity: a probe may combine a verb atom with the present-habitual template atom, because that lesson explicitly teaches the template as applying to any stem. HI-A1-F-32 is the only point that relies on it and says so. `derivedFrom` records each point's provenance -- the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or `hindi-specific` -- and is carried for auditability; no code reads it.

points.label: proper nouns: personal names, used in address and written into a form field
forms of address: the honorific -ji on a name or on a bare yes
place names: the city you live in, and the country
points.note: Covered by HI-C68-country, HI-C68-india and HI-C68-city: `desh`, the country name `Bharat`, and `shahar`, the form field both mocks' writing papers require. No settlement name below the country is taught, so a candidate can write the city LABEL but must supply their own city as a proper noun.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
grammatical gender is inherent: the -a/-i lean helps and then fails, so gender is learned with the word
gender by heteronymy for people: pita/mata, bhai/bahin, beta/beti
number: forming the plural of a masculine -a noun, a feminine -i noun, and a consonant-final noun
points.note: No atom teaches plural morphology; `log` ('people') is introduced as a lexical item and nothing else. Mock 1 item 16 and mock 2 item 20 both turn on `do bhashaen bolti hai`.

points.label: the oblique form a noun takes before a postposition (larka -> larke ko)
points.note: No Spanish counterpart: Spanish nouns do not inflect for case. The corpus teaches `me` and the `ka` genitive but never the case change the noun in front of them undergoes.

points.label: a numeral stands in front of the noun it counts (ek chay)
Hindi has no article: definiteness is carried by bareness, by ek, and by a demonstrative
points.note: The single largest structural difference from the proxy language, and the corpus never states it. Spanish spends four A1 points on the article; a learner arriving from English or Spanish needs to be told once that Hindi has none and what does the work instead. `ek chay dijiye` is taught, but as a cafe formula, not as indefiniteness.

points.label: the demonstratives yah and vah, and Hindi's two-way near/far split
a demonstrative used adnominally, in front of its noun (yah kitab)
points.note: The deixis chapter teaches yah and vah as standalone pronouns -- 'this one', 'that one' -- and never puts either in front of a noun.

points.label: possessive mera, and its agreement mera / meri / mere with the thing owned
possessive apka for the respectful addressee
the remaining possessives: uska, hamara, tumhara
points.note: Only mera and apka are introduced. A learner cannot say whose anything is unless it is their own or the addressee's.

points.label: the reflexive possessive apna, which replaces the possessive when the owner is the subject
points.note: Hindi's counterpart to Spanish reflexive `se`, and it is not optional: `main mera dost` is wrong where `main apna dost` is right. BOTH mocks' personal accounts use it -- `apne dost ke sath`, `apne parivar ke sath` -- and nothing in the corpus introduces it.

points.label: an attributive adjective stands in front of its noun
-a adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number
invariable adjectives that never change shape (lal, safed, thik)
predicative use: an adjective plus the copula (main thik hun)
relational adjectives naming origin or nationality (bharatiya, hindustani)
points.note: `Bharat` is now taught as a country NAME (HI-C68-india). The relational adjective built from it is not, and neither is any other nationality word, so this point measures exactly the derivation that is missing.

points.label: the intensifier bahut, and kafi
points.note: `bahut` is taught in HI-C71-very, which is the intensifier this point is about and the direct counterpart of the proxy's `muy`. `kafi` is still untaught; it is a second exponent of the same demand, not a second demand.

points.label: kam and zyada as everyday quantifiers
thoda as a hedging quantifier
points.note: Mock 1 listening item 12 keys on `han, thodi`.

points.label: comparison: X is bigger than Y
points.note: Hindi compares with the postposition `se`, which is untaught. See HI-A1-POST-04.

points.label: first-person singular main
second person: choosing between respectful ap and familiar tum
third person yah and vah used as subject pronouns
the subject pronoun paradigm as a whole, including ham and the plural third person
points.note: `ham` is never introduced -- mock 2 reading item 10 is `ham station par milenge` -- and neither is the plural `ve`. Three of the paradigm's slots are taught and the rest are absent.

points.label: the oblique first person mujhe, when the sentence will not let you be its subject
the other oblique pronouns: apko, use, hamen, tumhen
points.note: Only mujhe is introduced, and only as part of the pasand frame rather than as a paradigm.

points.label: a pronoun in front of a postposition (mere liye, mere sath, mere pas)
points.note: Hindi's counterpart to the proxy's stressed post-prepositional pronouns. Needs the oblique possessive plus a compound postposition, and neither is taught.

points.label: the y- / v- / k- system: one stem set gives near, far and interrogative
points.note: No Spanish counterpart. Spanish's deictic series are three unrelated stems; Hindi's are one machine with a swappable first consonant, and the corpus teaches it as such.

points.label: the relative pronoun jo, and the jo/vo correlative pair
points.note: Hindi relativises with a correlative pair rather than a single relative word, so this is the k-/j-/v- machine again one rung up. Neither `jo` nor the pattern is introduced.

points.label: the exclamative: kitna accha!
points.note: `kitna` is introduced only inside the memorised age question.

points.label: the numerals one to ten
the irregular numerals eleven to twenty
the numerals twenty-one to one hundred
points.note: The corpus stops at bis. Mock 2 reading item 4 prices tea at `pachas rupaye`, and no price, no age over twenty and no house number can be read or said.

points.label: the ordinals to tenth (pahla, dusra, tisra), and the distributive ek ... dusra
points.note: Not one ordinal is introduced, so nothing can be put in sequence -- no first floor, no second platform, no 'one ... the other'.

points.label: the Devanagari digits 0-9 as written on signs and forms
points.note: No Spanish counterpart: Spanish uses the same digits the learner already has. Hindi does not, and no atom introduces the Devanagari digit shapes. Both mocks render times and quantities in words, which conceals the gap rather than closing it.

points.label: measures of size, distance and weight
points.note: Size is taught (bara, chhota). Distance needs `dur`/`pas` and weight needs a unit; neither exists.

points.label: mathematics: the notion of number itself
the -na infinitive names the verb and yields the stem
the present copula hona: hun, hai, hain
the copula with tum: ho
points.note: `ho` occurs inside the age frame but no atom introduces the tum copula, so nothing demonstrates it independently of that one memorised question.

points.label: the present habitual: stem + -ta/-ti/-te + hona
the present habitual agrees twice: participle for gender and number, copula for person
negating a statement by putting nahin in front of the verb
the present continuous raha/rahi/rahe hai as a productive pattern
points.note: It appears twice as a fixed frame -- `ek baj raha hai` in the hour lesson, `barish ho rahi hai` in the weather lesson -- but no atom presents it as a pattern applying to any stem, the way the habitual lesson does for -ta.

points.label: the existential: X hai for 'there is'
possession: mere pas X hai
points.note: Hindi has no verb 'to have'; possession is `at me there is`, which needs `pas` and the oblique possessive. Neither is taught, so a learner cannot say they have anything.

points.label: recognising a future form in a set phrase (phir milenge)
forming the future productively: -unga / -ega / -engi and its agreement
points.note: Both mocks depend on it in the first scored part: mock 1 reading item 8 `main panch baje aunga`, item 11 `bas das minat me aegi`, mock 2 items 8 and 13. `milenge` is taught as one memorised farewell, not as a tense.

points.label: the past copula tha/thi, and the past habitual
points.note: Nothing in the corpus is past-tense. The proxy spends five A1 points on past morphology; Hindi needs at minimum `tha` to say where one was or what one used to do.

points.label: the perfective participle, its irregulars (kiya, gaya, diya), and the ne construction
points.note: Hindi's ergative `ne` has no Spanish counterpart and is the hardest single thing at this level, but the demand behind the proxy's preterite points is the same: report something that happened.

points.label: the perfect: participle plus hona
points.note: Downstream of the perfective participle, which is itself absent; see HI-A1-V-13.

points.label: the polite -iye imperative used for requests (dijiye, kijiye)
the plain and familiar imperatives (bol, bolo, boliye as a series)
points.note: Only the -iye form is introduced, and only inside two fixed courtesy phrases.

points.label: the negative imperative with mat
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 3 is exactly this: `yahan mat baithiye`.

points.label: the conjunctive participle -kar, Hindi's everyday clause-chainer
points.note: The load-bearing counterpart of the proxy's gerund. `kha kar`, `dekh kar`: Hindi chains events with it constantly and the corpus never introduces it.

points.label: noun + karna compound verbs (kam karna, madad karna, pasand karna)
points.note: No Spanish counterpart. Hindi makes most of its borrowed vocabulary verbal this way, and the corpus teaches the pattern explicitly.

points.label: the experiencer frame: mujhe X pasand hai, where the liked thing is the subject
chahiye for wanting and needing
points.note: Mock 1 reading item 12 `mujhe chay chahiye`, profile 2 `use pani chahiye`, mock 2 listening item 9. Nothing introduces it.

points.label: chahna, to want to do something
points.note: Distinct from chahiye (HI-A1-V-21): chahiye takes a noun, chahna takes another verb. Neither is introduced, so neither wanting a thing nor wanting to do something can be said.

points.label: sakna for ability and possibility
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 14 is `kya ap kal a sakte hain?`. The proxy spends four A1 points on ability and possibility; Hindi routes all four through this one verb, and it is absent.

points.label: janna, to know
points.note: The negation lesson's own example sentence is `main nahin janta`, so the learner meets the word, but no atom introduces it and it cannot be used affirmatively.

points.label: jana, and the go-somewhere frame every A1 routine description needs
points.note: Covered by productive combination, the same liberty `probeSemantics` names for HI-A1-F-32: HI-C69-go introduces `jana`, and the habitual template is introduced as applying to any stem, so `main steshan jata hun` is buildable from taught parts -- and HI-C69-go's guided practice says exactly that sentence.

points.label: khana and pina as verbs, distinguished from khana the noun
points.note: HI-C73-drink introduces `pina` and, in the same lesson, the doing-word sense of `khana` set against the noun the learner already holds. The lesson's wrap-up assesses the distinction the label asks for.

points.label: transitive sentences: a verb with an object
postpositions follow their noun where the proxy language would put a preposition in front
points.note: The structural inversion the proxy cannot express. Spanish has no postpositions at all.

points.label: me for location and containment
the genitive ka / ke / ki for possession and belonging
se for origin, instrument and means (Dilli se, bas se)
points.note: Load-bearing in both mocks: `Aman Dilli se hai`, `Ravi bas se school jata hai`, `ap kahan se hain?`, `main Bhopal se hun`, `train se kam par jata hai`. Never introduced, and the A1 speaking interview's origin question cannot be answered without it.

points.label: par for location at a point (ghar par, station par)
points.note: Mock 1 reading item 14 and mock 2 item 10 both turn on it.

points.label: ko marking an animate or definite object, and a recipient
points.note: The exact counterpart of the proxy's `a` before a human direct object -- the same demand, a different marker. Only the fused `mujhe` is present; `ko` itself is never introduced.

points.label: ke sath for accompaniment, and ke bina for its absence
points.note: Mock 1's account has `apne dost ke sath` and mock 2's has `apne parivar ke sath`.

points.label: spatial compound postpositions: ke pas, ke samne, ke piche
points.note: Mock 2 listening item 6 `bas station ke samne hai` and item 11 `nahin, pas hai`. The proxy spends three A1 points on relative position, distance and direction; Hindi routes all three through this construction and none of it is taught.

points.label: se ... tak for a span of days or hours
points.note: Mock 2's account opens `somvar se shukravar tak`. The weekday nouns are taught; the frame that spans them is not.

points.label: ke liye for purpose and benefit
points.note: The proxy expresses purpose with para plus an infinitive; Hindi uses the oblique infinitive plus ke liye. Neither the postposition nor the oblique infinitive is taught.

points.label: place deictics: yahan and vahan
time deictics: abhi, ab, and kal for both yesterday and tomorrow
aaj, the word for today
points.note: Taught in HI-C71-today, which places it beside the `kal` and `parson` the track already had. It carries mock 1 reading items 3 and 9 and listening item 6, mock 2 reading items 8 and 11, and the whole of mock 2's writing task, which is about why you cannot meet TODAY.

points.label: parson, the day after tomorrow
manner adverbs: jaldi and dhire
evaluative manner: doing something well, and doing it badly
points.note: `thik` and `achha` cover 'well'. No word for 'badly' -- neither `bura` nor `kharab` -- is introduced, so the proxy's bien/mal pair is half present and cannot be contrasted.

points.label: polarity adverbs: han and nahin
the additive bhi, Hindi's 'also' and 'too'
points.note: HI-C71-also teaches `bhi` and, because the placement is what beginners get wrong, teaches that it follows the word it adds to.

points.label: interrogative adverbs: kahan and kaise
short response adverbs: sach, bas, zarur, shayad, bilkul
kya as the content question word 'what'
kya in first position turning a statement into a yes/no question
points.note: The kya lesson teaches only the 'what' sense. Mock 1 listening item 12 and mock 2 reading item 14 both open with the polar kya, and it is the ordinary way an A1 interlocutor asks anything.

points.label: kaun for a person
kahan for a place
kaise / kaisa for manner and condition
kitna / kitne for quantity
kab for time
points.note: Taught in HI-C71-when, in its own lesson, alongside the five k- words the track already had.

points.label: kyon for reason, and kyonki for giving one
points.note: Taught in HI-C71-why. ONE atom carries both halves of the label: the lesson introduces `kyonki` inside the same block as `kyon`, as `kyon` plus `ki`, and its wrap-up assesses both meanings. A second atom would claim a second lesson that does not exist.

points.label: a question word sits in the clause's normal slot rather than being fronted
points.note: The deixis-system lesson generalises the k- shape but says nothing about where the question word goes. A probe must point at a claim the corpus makes, not at a pattern a reader might induce.

points.label: the tag question: ... hai na?
points.note: Hindi's counterpart to the proxy's confirmation tag, and the ordinary way to check a fact in conversation. Untaught.

points.label: nahin as the bare answer 'no'
ji han and ji nahin as the courteous answers
contrasting two alternatives negatively (X se nahin, Y se)
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 13 is `main bas se nahin, train se jaunga`. Needs `se`.

points.label: expressing ignorance: main nahin janta
points.note: Covered by an unusual route: the negation lesson's own worked example IS this sentence, so the learner is shown it complete. Recorded here rather than silently credited, because the atom is about the negator and the credit is for the example it carries.

points.label: the copular sentence: X Y hai
the verb comes last
points.note: Every taught sentence is verb-final, so the learner sees the order constantly, but no atom states it. The proxy's counterpart point is about word-order FLEXIBILITY; Hindi's is about a fixed position the learner must actively adopt, which is the larger demand of the two.

points.label: the vocative: addressing a named reader or hearer
points.note: The writing task in both mocks is addressed to a named person -- Reema, Mohan -- and the rubric awards 10 of that task's 60 points for a clear named reader. No atom covers address.

points.label: closing a written sentence with the danda
points.note: No Spanish counterpart -- the proxy's punctuation points are about the full stop, the comma and the inverted question mark. HI-W06-name-sentence-stop teaches the danda and declares an EMPTY `introduces` list, so it contributes no atom and cannot be probed. The gap is in the lesson's knowledge contract, not in the teaching.

points.label: producing a connected two-sentence message for a named reader
points.note: HI-W06-two-sentence-card and HI-W06-two-sentence-no-model teach it and, like HI-A1-S-04, declare empty introduces lists. The A1 writing paper's second task -- 30 to 40 words to a named reader, 60 of that paper's 100 points -- rests on this rung.

points.label: joining with aur
points.note: `aur` carries a clause join in five of the six mock profile texts. Never introduced.

points.label: the alternative ya
points.note: Mock 1 listening item 9 is `chay ya pani?`, and the A1 speaking task asks a preference by offering alternatives. Untaught.

points.label: the adversative lekin
points.note: Neither lekin nor par is introduced, so no taught sentence can be qualified or contradicted -- which also closes off the proxy's counter-argument function point.

points.label: the complementiser ki, for reporting what someone thinks or says
points.note: `sochna` and `samajhna` are taught as dictionary verbs, but with no `ki` there is no way to attach what is thought, so three of the proxy's opinion points have no Hindi route at all.

points.label: the infinitive as the subject or object of another verb
points.note: The infinitive itself IS taught (HI-A1-V-01), but only as the dictionary form. Nothing puts one inside another clause, and the verbs that would govern it -- chahna, sakna -- are absent.

points.label: jab for simultaneity, and the jab/tab correlative
points.note: The same correlative machine as `jo`/`vo` (HI-A1-PRON-09). Hindi is unusually systematic here and the corpus teaches the y-/v-/k- version of it, then stops.

points.label: the days of the week
the months of the year
the seasons
the parts of the day: subah, dopahar, sham, rat
telling the hour with bajna (ek baj raha hai)
naming a clock time as an appointment: X baje
points.note: The hour lesson teaches the predicate `ek baj raha hai` -- it IS one o'clock -- but not the adverbial `baje` that both mocks use throughout: `panch baje aunga`, `nau baje shuru hoga`, `sat baje uthti hun`, `char baje`. Reading the hour is taught; arranging to meet at it is not.

points.label: giving and asking an age
writing today's date
points.note: Mock 1's writing paper requires `aj ki tarikh` as one of six form fields worth 16 of that task's 40 content points. Neither `tarikh` nor a date format is taught, and the numerals above twenty needed to write one are absent too.

points.label: before and after: pahle and baad
points.note: Nothing can be sequenced in time.

points.label: the shirorekha head-line letters hang from
the abugida principle: a bare consonant already carries the inherent a
points.note: The deepest script difference from the proxy, which is alphabetic. Devanagari is an abugida and nothing in a Spanish inventory has anything to say about it.

points.label: matras replace the inherent vowel
the i-matra is written before the consonant it is pronounced after
the virama stops a consonant's vowel
conjunct consonants fuse a vowel-less consonant with the next
points.note: The nearest proxy point is the one about digraphs; conjuncts are a far larger demand, since Hindi builds hundreds of them and their shapes are not always predictable from the parts.

points.label: the nasalisation marks: candrabindu, and the anusvara it is confused with
points.note: Mapped to the proxy's diacritic point: both are a mark that changes a word without changing a letter.

points.label: word-final schwa is written and not said
the aspirated letters are distinct from their plain twins (bha/ba, kha/ka, dha/da)
a retroflex consonant is a different letter from its dental partner
the independent vowel letters a, aa and ii, for words that begin with a vowel
the remaining independent vowels: i, u, uu, e, ai, o, au
points.note: Only a, aa and ii have atoms. Seven of the ten are untaught, and A1 reading is unromanized by the track's own rule.

points.label: the matras aa, i, ii, u, e and ai
the remaining matras: uu, o, au and the vocalic ri
points.note: No atom introduces them, so a word as ordinary as `do` or `kaun` cannot be decoded from taught pieces.

points.label: the full consonant series, ka-varga through pa-varga and the semivowels and sibilants
points.note: The proxy's alphabet point, and the place the proxy most understates Hindi's demand. The track has letter atoms for eighteen consonants (na ma ka ta ra sa pa ha ya ca ssa la kha da dha bha ba retroflex-da). Fifteen more that ordinary A1 text needs -- ga gha cha ja jha retroflex-ta retroflex-tha retroflex-dha retroflex-na tha pha plain-ba va sha -- have none. Since the A1 reading paper forbids romanization, the letters with no atom are a hard ceiling on it.

points.label: the nuqta letters qa, kha, ga, za, fa and the flapped ra, rha
points.note: The single sharpest finding in this file, and one the proxy could never have surfaced. The corpus's own headwords are FULL of nuqta: shukriya, khushi, zarur, safed, darvaza, mez, sabzi, zyada, safar, tohfa, bukhar, fasal, khushbu, mulaqat. Learners are shown the letters constantly and never taught the mark.

points.label: Devanagari has no capital letters, so the proxy's capitalisation rules do not apply
points.note: Recorded rather than dropped, because a learner coming from a bicameral script has to be told once that sentence-initial and proper-noun capitals have no Devanagari equivalent. No atom says it.

points.label: writing a complete known sentence, with word spacing
completing a form field in Devanagari with no visible model
completing every field of an A1 practical form (name, city, language, time, drink, date)
points.note: The form rung proves exactly one field, the name. Both mocks' writing task 1 asks for six, and the rubric gives a blank field no content point.

points.label: the comma, and the question mark Hindi borrows from the Latin script
points.note: Hindi writes a question mark but never an opening one, and uses the Latin comma. Neither is introduced, and the danda (HI-A1-S-04) is the only terminator the corpus touches at all.

points.label: abbreviations and symbols on signs and forms
points.note: The rupee sign, `Dr.`, `No.`: nothing of the kind is taught, and the A1 reading paper opens on signs and form extracts.

points.label: the aspirated/unaspirated contrast changes the word
the retroflex/dental contrast changes the word
nasalised vowels
long and short vowels are different vowels
the borrowed consonants z, f and q as sounds, not just as spellings
points.note: The spoken twin of HI-A1-SCR-16.

points.label: rising intonation marks a yes/no question when no kya is present
points.note: No atom addresses intonation. The A1 listening paper plays every exchange as speech, and its polar questions are carried by intonation as often as by kya.

points.label: word stress and the rhythm of a phrase
points.note: Untreated in the corpus, and enumerated here for the same reason the Spanish inventory records its own pronunciation gap: no source draws an A1/A2 line for it, so drawing one ourselves would be the editorial promotion that file declines to make.

points.label: greet at any hour with namaste, and choose namaskar when the setting is formal
respond to a greeting
greet in the morning
greet in the afternoon
greet in the evening
wish someone good night
judge which greeting register a situation wants
points.note: Hindi's Sanskritic/Perso-Arabic register split has no Spanish A1 counterpart, and the corpus teaches it deliberately -- dhanyavad against shukriya, kripaya against dijiye.

points.label: take leave, formally and casually
propose closing the conversation
say you will see someone tomorrow
thank someone, choosing between the Sanskritic and the everyday word
answer thanks
apologise
say please in writing and on a sign
make a spoken request across a counter with the -iye form
give your name
ask someone's name
say you are pleased to meet someone
introduce a third person (ye mere dost hain)
points.note: Introducing oneself is taught; introducing somebody else needs the adnominal demonstrative (HI-A1-DET-03) and the honorific plural, and neither is.

points.label: ask how someone is
say how you are
say which language you speak
say where you live
ask where someone is from, and say where you are from
points.note: The first question of the A1 speaking interview and of mock 1 listening item 10. `desh` and `shahar` are now taught (HI-C68), so the ANSWER's content words exist; the frame still needs `se`, which is untaught.

points.label: say what work you do
give your age
give the rest of your personal data: surname, address, telephone number
points.note: Name and age are taught. No word for surname, address or telephone exists, and `shahar` -- a required field in both mocks' forms -- is not taught either.

points.label: confirm or deny what was just said
ask for an evaluation (kaisa hai?)
evaluate something as good, fine or correct
express certainty, and express doubt
ask for an opinion, and give one
points.note: Covered by productive combination, not by a single lesson: `sochna` is introduced, and the habitual template is introduced as applying to any stem, so `ap kya sochte hain?` is buildable from taught parts. Attaching the OPINION ITSELF is not -- that needs `ki`, and HI-A1-CJ-04 records it as missing.

points.label: show you are following what is said
say what you like
say what you prefer
points.note: The pasand lesson teaches `pasand karna` explicitly as the active choosing sense, nearer to 'I prefer' than to 'I like'.

points.label: ask a preference by offering alternatives
points.note: Needs `ya`. Mock 1 listening item 9 is `chay ya pani?`.

points.label: say what you want, and ask what someone wants
points.note: Needs `chahiye` or `chahna`; see HI-A1-V-21 and HI-A1-V-22.

points.label: ask about and state plans and intentions
points.note: Needs the productive future; see HI-A1-V-11.

points.label: ask whether someone knows something, and say you do
points.note: Needs `janna`; see HI-A1-V-24. The negative half of this pair IS reachable, which is why HI-A1-NEG-04 is covered and this is not.

points.label: ask about and express ability
points.note: Needs `sakna` or `ana`; see HI-A1-V-23.

points.label: give an instruction
respond to an order or request
grant permission
refuse permission
points.note: Needs the prohibitive `mat`; see HI-A1-V-17.

points.label: ask for help
offer and invite
points.note: The -iye form is taught only inside two fixed courtesy phrases, and no offer formula -- `chay lijiye`, `aiye` -- is introduced.

points.label: accept an offer or invitation
decline an offer or invitation
say why you cannot do something
points.note: Mock 2's writing task opens on it and needs `kyonki` plus a negated modal.

points.label: welcome someone
offer a good wish for the occasion
points.note: The proxy's exponent is a drinking toast, which is not the Hindi move. The transferable demand is a set-phrase well-wish, and the shubh- formulas are exactly that.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: `badhai ho` is the formula, and no lesson introduces it.

points.label: offer condolences
points.note: No condolence formula is taught. The track has a rich courtesy-noun chapter and no words for this occasion.

points.label: ask for a person and respond
points.note: Needs a calling formula and the honorific plural for a third person.

points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Needs the prohibitive; see HI-A1-V-17.

points.label: say you did not understand, and ask for a repetition
points.note: No Spanish A1 counterpart in the proxy's function list, but the A1 speaking construct scores interaction and REPAIR at 25 percent of every part, so it is a scored demand here. `samajhna` is taught as a dictionary verb and no atom builds the repair move.

points.label: point at a thing and ask what it is
describe the weather
describe a daily routine
points.note: The one-minute prepared description and the personal-account listening part in both mocks are routines. The habitual tense is taught, but `jana`, `uthna`, `baje`, `se` and `par` -- everything a routine is made of besides the tense -- are not.

points.label: read a public sign: entrance, exit, open, closed
points.note: Exactly the four words the label names, taught in HI-C74-open, HI-C74-closed, HI-C74-entrance and HI-C74-exit. These carry items 1 to 4 of both mocks' reading papers.

points.label: read a practical form's field labels and say which field holds what
ask what something costs
points.note: HI-C72-price teaches `dam` and builds `dam kya hai?` from it and the already-taught `kya`, and the lesson's guided practice and wrap-up both require the learner to produce that question. The exponent taught is `dam kya hai?`, NOT the `kitne ka` the earlier note named; both are current market Hindi. STATING an answer still needs numerals above twenty, which HI-A1-NUM-03 records as missing.

points.label: ask when something happens
points.note: Needs `kab`; see HI-A1-Q-07.

points.label: propose meeting again
propose a specific day, time and place to meet
points.note: The writing task in BOTH mocks ends on it. `kal milte hain` proposes a day and nothing else; the time needs `baje` and the place needs `par` or `me` with a place noun the corpus does not have.

points.label: sight and looking
hearing and listening
colour
attractiveness: beautiful and ugly
points.note: Neither `sundar` nor any opposite is introduced.

points.label: interest
points.note: Nothing expresses finding something interesting or dull. pasand (HI-A1-F-34) covers liking and stops there.

points.label: ease and difficulty
points.note: `asan` and `mushkil` are both untaught, so a learner cannot say the language is hard.

points.label: reflection and knowledge
parts of the body
physical characteristics of a person
points.note: `bara` and `chhota` are taught for things. No word for tall, short, thin or heavy, and the `purana` lesson says explicitly that it is used of things and not of people.

points.label: actions and positions of the body
character and personality adjectives
points.note: Only `achha`. Nothing describes a person's disposition.

points.label: personal identity: name and age
documents: passport and identity card
points.note: Untaught. The A1 reading paper opens on form extracts, which is the setting these words belong to.

points.label: personal objects
family relationships
social relationships: friend, neighbour, guest
celebrations and social occasions
the meals of the day
points.note: `nashta` ('breakfast') is now taught in HI-C73-breakfast, and the doing-word sense of `khana` is taught in HI-C73-drink and covered at HI-A1-V-26. Lunch and dinner are still unnamed, so two thirds of the label's demand remains.

points.label: drink
foodstuffs
dishes and courses
the eating place: ordering, the server, the bill
points.note: Ordering was already taught (HI-A1-F-15). HI-C73 adds `hotal` for the eating house, `bil` for the bill and `vetar` for the server, which are the three the label names.

points.label: educational institutions
points.note: `school` appears in four separate mock items across the two papers and is introduced nowhere.

points.label: teaching staff and students
learning and teaching
teaching materials and classroom furniture
the education system: timetable, examinations and marks
points.note: Teacher and student are taught (HI-A1-LEX-24) and nothing that surrounds them is. Mock 1 listening item 5 is a class starting at nine.

points.label: classroom language
points.note: The directions a candidate reads on the paper itself. From A2 onward the track's own assessment spec says directions are in Hindi, so this becomes load-bearing one level up.

points.label: professions and posts
workplaces, tools and work clothing
working activity
unemployment, job-seeking, and rights at work
points.note: Untaught. The proxy places these at A1; whether they belong at A1 in Hindi is a judgement this file does not make, so the point is enumerated and left unmapped rather than dropped.

points.label: free time and entertainment
points.note: HI-C70 teaches `khel`, `khelna` and `aram`, which answer playing and resting. An outing is still unnamed.

points.label: sport and games
points.note: HI-C70 teaches the game, the doing word and `kriket` itself, which is the game mock 2's listening profile has Imran playing.

points.label: written correspondence
points.note: The A1 writing paper's main task IS a written message, and no word for letter, message or note is taught.

points.label: media, telephone, press, broadcast and the internet
points.note: Wholly untaught. The proxy spends five A1 points here; the A1 form asks for a telephone number and the track has no word for a telephone.

points.label: types and parts of a dwelling
household objects and furniture
domestic activities
buying, selling and renting a home
points.note: The dwelling and its parts are well taught (HI-A1-LEX-37). A verb of buying now exists -- `kharidna`, HI-C72-buy -- but nothing sells or rents, and no dwelling transaction is taught, so this point stays uncovered on its own terms.

points.label: health and illness
hygiene
health services, centres and medicines
points.note: The symptoms are taught and the doctor, the clinic and the medicine are not, so the vocabulary stops exactly where a learner would need to act on it.

points.label: postal, financial, protection and security services
points.note: Untaught. These are the everyday errands an A1 learner in-country actually runs.

points.label: places, people and activities of shopping
clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: `kapra` is taught as the material, cloth. No garment, no footwear.

points.label: payment: money, price and change
points.note: HI-C72 teaches `paisa`, `rupaya` and `dam`. The numerals above twenty that the cafe role-play needs to STATE a price are still missing and are enumerated at HI-A1-NUM-03; this point covers the vocabulary of payment, not the ability to say every amount.

points.label: transport: bus, train, bicycle, station
points.note: HI-C69 teaches `gari`, `rel`, `steshan` and `tikat`, and `bas` was already taught. A bicycle is still not named, so the label's fourth item is the one gap left.

points.label: travel objects, documents and accommodation
points.note: safar (a journey) and mulaqat (a meeting) are taught as abstractions. Nothing packs, books or stays anywhere.

points.label: commerce, businesses, industry and energy
points.note: Untaught, and plausibly above A1 in practice; enumerated because the proxy places it at A1 and this file does not silently overrule the proxy on level.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: Untaught. The corpus is a deliberately traditional village-and-household lexicon, which is a coherent choice and still leaves this A1 domain empty.

points.label: government, politics and the law
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: the arts: music, dance, image, literature, stage and screen
points.note: `gana` is now taught in HI-C70-song, as both the song and the singing, so the music corner of this label has a foothold. Dance, image, literature, stage and screen are all still untaught; the proxy spends six A1 points here and one word does not answer them.

points.label: religion and observance
points.note: One of the few domains where the track is RICHER than the proxy: blessing, garland, oil lamp and the bow are all taught, and the greeting chapter's etymologies are about the gesture.

points.label: the universe and the sky
geography: country, town, city, capital
points.note: `gaon` was already taught; `desh`, `Bharat` and `shahar` are now taught in HI-C68. The word for a capital is still not, which is the remaining quarter of this point's label.

points.label: urban and rural spaces
climate and weather
fauna
flora
naming a second language, and naming nationalities
points.note: `bhasha` and `angrezi` are taught in HI-C68-language and HI-C68-english, which is what mock 1 item 16 and mock 2 item 20 key on and what the writing papers' `bhasha` field needs. Naming a NATIONALITY still needs the relational adjective, which stays untaught and is enumerated separately at HI-A1-ADJ-05.

points.label: the words a town sign or a station announcement uses
points.note: HI-C74 teaches `khula`, `band`, `pravesh`, `nikas` and `der`, and HI-C69 teaches `steshan`. Six of the nine words this note used to list. `dhyan den`, `shuru`, `taiyar` and `platform` are still untaught.

points.label: courtesy nouns
points.note: The track teaches a whole chapter of abstract courtesy nouns -- gratitude, favour, respect, kindness, entreaty, permission, manners -- which the proxy has no A1 counterpart for.

points.label: everyday action verbs
verbal expression: speaking and writing
